name: Renal / ureteric colic

matching.reasoningTemplate: Severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with haematuria and no fever suggests a stone.

redFlags: Fever with obstruction → emergency (infected obstructed system)

clinicalPearls: Renal colic is classic visceral pain from distention of a hollow viscus (the obstructed collecting system/ureter): cramping and intermittent rather than constant (p.551).
Stones obstructing urinary flow are the single most important risk factor for perinephric/renal abscess; 20-60% of patients with perinephric abscess have renal stones (p.1118).

Urea-splitting organisms (notably Proteus, also other urease producers) alkalinize the urine, favoring precipitation of struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) and carbonate-apatite, which can form staghorn calculi in the renal pelvis (p.1118, p.1334).
Struvite stones act as a persistent nidus for recurrent UTI and typically cannot be eradicated by antibiotics alone without removal of the stone (p.1118, p.1334).

Stone-associated obstruction is a recognized cause of postrenal azotemia/AKI; because one functioning kidney clears adequately, obstructive renal failure from stones generally requires bilateral ureteric obstruction or unilateral obstruction in a solitary/single functioning kidney (p.383).
Nephrolithiasis can be the presenting feature of an underlying metabolic disorder such as primary hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia (p.406).
Imaging of the upper tracts is advised in any patient with hematuria, a history of calculi, or prior urinary tract problems (p.747).
harrison.pathophysiology: Colicky flank pain arises from acute distention of the renal collecting system and ureter when a stone obstructs urinary outflow, producing visceral cramping pain (p.551). Obstruction proximal to the bladder produces hydroureter and renal pelvic dilation (hydronephrosis); if unrelieved this impairs glomerular filtration and causes postrenal azotemia (p.383). In urease-producing infection (e.g., Proteus), hydrolysis of urea to ammonia raises urinary pH; the resulting alkaline environment precipitates struvite and carbonate-apatite, building staghorn calculi that perpetuate infection and obstruction (p.1118, p.1334). Stones also serve as a chronic nidus that promotes recurrent and recalcitrant urinary infection (p.1118).
additionalDifferentials: Ruptured/impending-rupture abdominal aortic aneurysm — abdominal pain radiating to the flank, sacral region, or genitalia should always raise suspicion of a leaking AAA; pain may precede rupture by days (p.154).
Acute mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion to exam in a vascular patient) (p.154).

Other causes of acute lower abdominal pain such as appendicitis, salpingitis, ectopic pregnancy, inguinal hernia, inflammatory bowel disease, and bowel obstruction (p.18 abdominal pain differential table).
Ureteric obstruction due to extrinsic malignancy (pelvic/prostatic/gynecologic tumors, retroperitoneal nodes) or post-radiation ureteric fibrosis, which can mimic stone-related obstruction (p.631).
infectionMimics: Perinephric or renal abscess — flank/abdominal pain, fever in at least half; suspect when pyelonephritis remains febrile after 4-5 days, when urine culture is polymicrobial, when stones are known, or when fever and pyuria coexist with a sterile urine culture (p.1118).
nonInfectiousMimics: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with flank/genital radiation, especially in older patients (p.154).
Ureteric obstruction from malignancy or retroperitoneal fibrosis presenting with flank pain (p.631).
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasonography — useful to identify hydronephrosis/ureteric and pelvic dilation, though it may be falsely negative early or when ureteric dilation is prevented (e.g., retroperitoneal fibrosis or tumor encasement) (p.383, p.631).
Abdominal CT and renal ultrasound are the most useful modalities when perinephric/renal abscess is suspected (p.1118).

Urinalysis showing alkaline urine plus a urease-producing organism (e.g., Proteus) may prompt evaluation for urolithiasis, though Harrison notes clinical support for routine action on this finding is lacking (p.1334).
Serum calcium / PTH and metabolic workup when an underlying stone-promoting metabolic disorder (e.g., primary hyperparathyroidism) is suspected (p.406).
redFlags: Pain radiating to flank, sacral region, or genitalia in an older patient — exclude a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (p.154).
Rising serum creatinine, oliguria, or anuria — suggests obstruction of a solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction and warrants immediate evaluation (p.383, p.631).

Persistent fever after several days of treatment for presumed pyelonephritis, polymicrobial urine, or fever/pyuria with sterile culture — suspect perinephric/renal abscess complicating an obstructing stone (p.1118).
harrison.prognosis: Stone-related obstruction is usually reversible if relieved promptly; urinary tract obstruction accounts for under 5% of acute renal failure and must be excluded early because it is correctable (p.383). When obstruction is complicated by infection (abscess), diagnosis is frequently delayed and mortality is appreciable, though lower than historically (p.1118). Struvite/staghorn stones tend to recur and perpetuate infection unless the stone is removed (p.1118, p.1334).
pitfalls: Assuming flank pain radiating to the groin is always a stone — in older patients a ruptured/leaking AAA can present identically and is rapidly fatal if missed (p.154).
Relying on a negative ultrasound to exclude obstruction; dilation may be absent early or when the ureter cannot distend (p.383).
Failing to recognize an infected obstructed system / perinephric abscess in a patient with known stones who stays febrile or has polymicrobial or sterile-but-pyuric urine (p.1118).
Overlooking an underlying metabolic cause (e.g., hyperparathyroidism) in a stone former (p.406).
